source.title: Towards understanding epoch-wise double descent in two-layer linear neural networks

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study derives and simulates epoch-wise generalisation-error curves for decoupled two-layer linear networks, a different model and approach from empirical deep-network double-descent studies.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports simulated generalisation MSE curves under parameter sweeps. The text states that double descent appears for large input-covariance eigenvalues in all three dynamics settings, and for large input-output covariance singular values only when η > 0. The figure's exact numerical curve values are not stated. Claims cited from earlier work are not recorded as results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study derives and simulates the generalisation error over gradient-flow time in decoupled two-layer linear networks. It shows when a fall-rise-fall curve can arise, which bears on V2 in a different, analytically tractable model. The simulations are hand-built to show that the pattern is possible: parameters are chosen and weights duplicated. They show existence and conditions, not how often the pattern occurs.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. In decoupled two-layer linear networks, epoch-wise double descent is a superposition of per-weight bias-variance curves. Besides input-covariance eigenvalues, singular values of the input-output covariance can cause it. The authors derive necessary conditions and show an extra scenario possible in the two-layer model but not the one-layer model. They present this as a step toward understanding deep models, not a test of them.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses theoretical gradient-flow analysis and parameterized simulations in a decoupled two-layer linear network, rather than empirical sweeps over epochs in deep nonlinear networks.
record.method_sensitivity: The pattern varies with input-covariance eigenvalues, input-output-covariance singular values, and the dynamics parameters γ and η; the reported λ_i threshold shifts with γ, and the σ_i effect is reported only when η > 0.

fits_no_version.finding: In the decoupled linear model, epoch-wise double descent can only arise as a superposition of per-weight curves, each monotone or U-shaped. Proposition 3 gives a necessary condition: an inflection point must lie between the per-weight minima times. The two-layer model allows a second scenario that the one-layer model does not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Epoch-wise double descent arises from overlapping bias-variance curves of features learned at different speeds, set by input eigenvalues and, in deeper linear nets, by input-output singular values. It is not caused by capacity crossing the sample size.

record.problems: The results rely on decoupled dynamics, spectral alignment assumptions, and an approximation of the true input covariance by the sample covariance. Figure 1 provides qualitative curves without exact numerical values, and no uncertainty estimates are stated.

untested.parts: Deep nonlinear networks, real datasets and SGD with discrete epochs. The study uses continuous gradient flow in a decoupled linear model with synthetic spectra. It also does not vary label noise (ρ, the noise model) as a driver.
Sample size is not varied. The analysis assumes a large sample, so the sample covariance approximates the true one.
There is no effective-complexity measure. The mechanism offered is differing learning speeds, not capacity.
The roles of noise and regularisation in the peak are not tested.

missing.what: The analytic results (Proposition 2, Proposition 3, Corollary 1) are not recorded as rows: the error is a sum of monotone or U-shaped curves, and a necessary condition for double descent is stated. Under the one-layer dynamics only one scenario is possible, and it depends on λ but not σ.
The statement that large eigenvalue or singular-value differences let one curve dominate and hide the double descent, so the simulations duplicate weights.

record.verdict_notes: The simulations are illustrative existence demonstrations built from chosen parameters (ρ_i=0.5, ρ_j=0.8, multiplicity 9/1). The figure gives no numeric values. The 'challenges' label on r4 in the record is wrong: V2 does not say the σ-driven pattern must appear in the one-layer model, so r4 falls under limits_scope. The study's mechanism (differing learning speeds; overparameterisation not needed, per its citations) sits outside the capacity-based account of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Model-wise behavior as model size grows.
The study examines continuous gradient-flow time in a decoupled two-layer linear model, not empirical epoch sweeps in deep nonlinear networks.
Changing training sample size near an interpolation threshold.
Capacity-wise double descent across model classes.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across axes.
The paper does not test label-noise or variance as a peak driver, multiple descent peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Recounting complexity using an effective number of parameters.

relationships.reason: The pattern needs suitable differences in λ or σ across weights, not too large. The σ_i route is absent in the one-layer case (r4) and the λ_i threshold shifts with γ (r1–r3). relationships.display_finding: The pattern required suitably sized differences in λ or σ across weights; large differences let one curve obscure it, the σ mechanism vanished with one layer, and the λ threshold varied with γ.

tranche.reason: Closed-form gradient-flow analysis and constructed simulations address epoch-wise double descent using a different method in decoupled linear networks.

source_check.notes: Figure 1 uses 10 active weights with deliberately chosen multiplicities: zi:zj is 9:1 for λ_i sweeps and 1:9 for σ_i sweeps. The theoretical conditions are necessary, not sufficient; spectral concealment is a tendency, not a universal upper bound.
